parts.title: Booking a ski holiday
parts.context: A man books a skiing trip for a group of friends.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a travel agency to book a skiing trip for a group of friends. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Snowline Travel, Anna speaking.

script.speaker: chris
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book a ski holiday, please. It's for a group of friends, and we try to go away together every winter.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: That sounds fun. I'll take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The trip is for a group of friends, so 'friends' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Could I have your surname, please?

script.speaker: chris
script.text: It's Sherwood. That's S-H-E-R-W-O-O-D.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Thank you, Mr Sherwood. How many of you will there be?

script.speaker: chris
script.text: There were eight of us, but two have pulled out, so it's six.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: And where would you like to go?

script.speaker: chris
script.text: We'd like to go to Austria. We went to France last year, and it was very expensive.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: When would you like to travel?

script.speaker: chris
script.text: The seventh of February, for a week.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: What is the level of your group?

script.speaker: chris
script.text: Most of us are beginners, I'm afraid. Only two have been skiing before.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: We have three packages. The Standard package is sixty-five pounds a night. It includes breakfast, and a bus pass, so you can travel between the villages without paying.

script.speaker: chris
script.text: That sounds good. What about the next one?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: The Comfort package is eighty pounds a night, with breakfast and dinner, and the hire of all your ski equipment, which saves a lot of money.

script.speaker: chris
script.text: Most of us don't have our own skis, so that sounds right.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: The Luxury package is ninety-five pounds a night. It includes everything in the Comfort package, plus access to the spa, with a sauna and a pool, which is lovely after a day on the slopes.

script.speaker: chris
script.text: I think Comfort is best for us. Are lessons included?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Not in the price, but you can book them at the resort. I'd recommend a lesson every morning for the beginners.

script.speaker: chris
script.text: Thank you. Can I pay a deposit now?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Yes, I'll send you a form by email this afternoon.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A ski resort briefing
parts.context: A resort manager gives guests information and safety advice.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a ski resort manager giving a safety and information briefing. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Alpenhof. I'm Hans Tanner, the resort manager, and I'll tell you what you need to know before you hit the slopes. Please look at the map. We're in the village, at the bottom, and the main path leads up the mountain.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: Just by the entrance, on the right, is ski hire, where you collect your skis and boots. On the left, at the bottom, is the ski school, where the beginners' lessons begin at nine. Between the ski school and the path is the first aid post, which is staffed all day.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: Going up the path, on the left is the beginners' area, with a gentle slope and a magic carpet lift. On the right is the Sun Hut café, which serves hot chocolate and the best apple cake in the Alps.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: At the top of the path is the gondola station, which takes you up to the main slopes. And to the right of it is a viewpoint, with a wonderful view of the glacier, though you'll need a gondola ticket to get there.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: Some practical points. A day pass for the lifts costs forty-five euros, and a six-day pass is cheaper, if you're staying all week.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: The last gondola down leaves at half past four. Please don't miss it, because the walk down takes more than two hours, and it gets dark quickly in the mountains.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: Helmets are compulsory for children under fourteen. Adults are not required to wear them, but we strongly recommend it, and you can hire one at the same desk as your skis.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: Look out for the coloured flags at the top of each slope. A green flag means the slope is open, and a red flag means it is closed. Never ski on a closed slope, however good the snow looks.

script.speaker: tanner
script.text: If you see an accident, or if you have one, please report it at the nearest lift station, where staff will call the mountain rescue. Have a wonderful week, and ski safely.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Designing a vocabulary game
parts.context: Two education students describe a board game for children.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two education students, Mia and Ravi, designing a vocabulary board game for children. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: Ravi, shall we describe our game in the report? It's a board game to help children learn French vocabulary.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Yes. I think we should say clearly who it's for. I'd say seven to nine-year-olds, because the five- and six-year-olds can't read the cards yet, and the older ones would find it too easy.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: Agreed. Why did we decide on vocabulary, and not grammar?

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Because it's easy to test. You can see straight away whether a child knows a word, but grammar is much harder to assess in a game.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: How many words did we include?

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Eighty, in groups of ten, such as animals, food and colours.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: What did the teacher say about the first version?

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: That it was too long. Children lost interest after twenty minutes, so we shortened the board.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: And how are we going to test the game?

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: In a real class, at the primary school in Hill Street. Mrs Evans has agreed to let us try it with a group of twelve children.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: Now let me describe how the game works. First, each player puts a counter on the start square.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: Then they roll a dice and move that number of squares along the board.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: If they land on a coloured square, they pick up a card with a picture on it, such as an apple or a cat.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: They have to say the French word before the timer runs out. We use a one-minute sand timer, which the children like.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: If they're correct, they win a point, and the player with the most points at the end wins the game.

script.speaker: ravi
script.text: There's no prize, although the teacher said she might give out stickers.

script.speaker: mia
script.text: That's a nice idea. Shall I draw the board for the appendix?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the Industrial Revolution
parts.context: A history lecture on the Industrial Revolution.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the Industrial Revolution. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Few periods in history changed everyday life as much as the Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the late eighteenth century, and then spread across the world.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The first great change came in the textile industry. Until then, cloth was made by hand at home, in a slow process. A series of inventions changed this. The spinning jenny, invented in the seventeen sixties, allowed a single worker to spin several threads at once, and later machines made spinning and weaving faster still. As machines became larger, they were moved into factories.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The other key invention was the steam engine. James Watt greatly improved the design in the seventeen sixties, and his engines were soon used to power factories, mines and ships. They were driven by coal, which Britain had in large quantities, and the demand for coal and iron grew rapidly.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Transport changed too. Canals, and then railways, made it cheaper and faster to move goods and people. The first public railway to use steam locomotives opened in eighteen twenty-five, and within a few decades, a network covered the country.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Cities grew at an astonishing speed. Towns such as Manchester, which had been small, became huge, as people left the countryside to find work in the factories. But the new towns were crowded and dirty, with few sewers and little clean water, and diseases spread quickly.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Working conditions were harsh. Many factory workers were children, who worked long hours for little pay. Public concern led Parliament to pass a series of laws, called the Factory Acts, which gradually limited the hours of children and improved safety.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Historians still debate whether ordinary people benefited. In the short term, many suffered. But in the long run, living standards rose, and the Industrial Revolution laid the foundation for modern economic growth. Next week we'll look at the changes in agriculture.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
